doc.title: Yusef Lateef — Smithsonian Jazz Oral History

chapter: Flute, world instruments and first recordings
title: Flute, oboe and instruments from other cultures
summary: Flute was rare in jazz; he describes taking up the oboe, finding the arghul, rebab and making bamboo flutes to widen his expression.

story.theme_name: The reed and horn player's craft: clarinet, sax, tone
story.community_name: Reeds, mouthpieces and horns: the reed player's gear

blocks.x: Mmhmm. Now, at that time, that was still, flute in the music was still kind of...I’d say rare, not exotic, but rare.
There weren’t a lot of people doubling at that point.
That’s true. Well, but if you look at some of those old pictures of Chick Webb’s band, you’ll see flutes on the bandstand.
On the bandstand, sure. Yeah. Bass clarinets, and all that.
That’s right, and, of course, what’s his name, Frank uh Wess...
...played flute in the ‘40s when he was with the [Billy] Eckstine band.
Well, what did, what did you find uh flute brought to your uh your arsenal, for want of a better word?

Well, the, the reason I appreciated playing the flute is because after I made my first personal recording in ’55, I realized that, if I should continue to record, that I would have the vary of the canvas of my expression. So, being able to play flute helped me do that, and the oboe, of course, then I started looking, started studying music of other cultures. I wasn’t able to travel abroad, but I could go to the library and study scores and records, and I, I did as much of that as I could. Um and then I found like a...the arghul, which is a Syrian, double-reed instrument, I found that it on the eastern market in Detroit, in a Syrian spice store. Uh...I, while working at Chrysler’s between ’50 and ’55, I met um a Syrian person uh who introduced me to the rebab, which is a one-stringed fiddle. Uh...each middle-eastern country, farsian country, they have their one-stringed fiddle, and even in Africa. It goes by different names. Anyway, it’s reported that the rebab was played by King David when he said his prayers about 5000 years ago. So, he made me that and um Ernie Farrell played it. I remember the first piece where we used the rebab was called Morning. It was 1955 on Savoy Records. Um then I started making flutes, after I started studying the Germanic sea flute. I’d make them out of bamboo, and I used a lot of them in some compositions. Um for example, the piece A Long Time Ago.

I used a couple of bamboo flutes that I had made by hand. Um I remember working at Ronnie Scott’s [Jazz Club] in England, and uh a Chinese fellow gave me a Buddhist Temple flute, which I still have, and I used in a composition called The African- American Epic Suite for quartet and orchestra. It’s kind of a fetish to, to discover flutes and make them. Like Max [Roach] said, we’re “sound merchants” [chuckling].
